modules.title: Python Basics
modules.blurb: Values, variables, and your first programs.

lessons.title: Hello, Python
body: Python is a clear, readable language used for web apps, data, automation, and AI.
The classic first program prints a message to the screen.
lessons.tip: print() is a built-in function. Text inside quotes is a string.

lessons.title: Variables & Types
body: A variable stores a value under a name. Python figures out the type for you.
Common types: int, float, str, and bool.
lessons.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
pi = 3.14
is_coder = True
print(name, age, pi, is_coder)
lessons.tip: Use snake_case for variable names: total_score, not totalScore.

lessons.title: Working with Strings
body: Strings can be combined (concatenated) and formatted with f-strings.
f-strings let you embed expressions inside curly braces.
lessons.code:
city = "Lisbon"
year = 2026
print(f"Coding from {city} in {year}")
print("Py" + "thon".upper())
lessons.tip: Prefer f-strings over + for readable text assembly.

quiz.q: Which call prints text to the console?

modules.title: Control Flow
modules.blurb: Make decisions and repeat work with if and loops.

lessons.title: If / Elif / Else
body: Conditionals run code only when a condition is true.
Compare with ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=. Combine with and, or, not.
lessons.tip: Indentation (usually 4 spaces) defines blocks in Python.

lessons.title: For & While Loops
body: for walks through a sequence. while repeats until a condition fails.
range(n) gives numbers from 0 up to (but not including) n.
lessons.tip: Avoid infinite while loops — always update the condition.

lessons.title: Break & Continue
body: break exits a loop early. continue skips to the next iteration.
Use them sparingly when they make intent clearer.
lessons.tip: 3 is skipped by continue; 5 never prints because of break.

modules.title: Data Structures
modules.blurb: Lists, dictionaries, and the collections you’ll use every day.

lessons.title: Lists
body: A list is an ordered, mutable collection. Index from 0.
append adds an item; slicing copies a stretch of items.
lessons.tip: Negative indexes count from the end: -1 is the last item.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
body: Dicts map keys to values. Lookups by key are fast and readable.
Keys are usually strings; values can be any type.
lessons.tip: .get(key, default) avoids KeyError when a key might be absent.

lessons.title: List Comprehensions
body: Comprehensions build lists in one expressive line.
They can include a filter with if.
lessons.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
squares = [n * n for n in nums]
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
print(squares)
print(evens)
lessons.tip: Keep comprehensions short — long ones are clearer as normal loops.

quiz.q: How do you add an item to a list?
What is [n for n in range(3)]?

modules.title: Functions
modules.blurb: Package logic into reusable, testable pieces.

lessons.title: Defining Functions
body: def names a function. Parameters receive inputs; return sends a result back.
Call the function by writing its name followed by parentheses.
lessons.code:
def greet(name):
    return f"Welcome, {name}!"

print(greet("PyTrail"))
print(greet("friend"))
lessons.tip: Functions should do one clear job and return early when possible.

lessons.title: Defaults & Keyword Args
body: Default parameter values make calls optional and friendlier.
Keyword arguments document intent at the call site.
lessons.code:
def power(base, exp=2):
    return base ** exp

print(power(5))
print(power(2, exp=10))
lessons.tip: Put parameters with defaults after required ones.

lessons.title: Scope Basics
body: Names assigned inside a function are local unless declared otherwise.
Prefer passing values in and returning results over global state.
lessons.code:
rate = 1.1

def with_tax(price):
    return price * rate

print(with_tax(100))
lessons.tip: Floats are approximate — for money, prefer decimal later on.
